connector: Yesterday you saw how fast the war spread across Europe. Today we stop in one small country: Denmark, the place where Number the Stars happens. Germany took it over in a single day in April 1940. What was life like for the Danish people after that? Watch the small details. They say a lot.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome back. Today we zoom in on one country, the one our new book is set in: Denmark. Germany took it over in a single day. So what was everyday life like after that? You’ll warm up, work with some words, then read about Denmark under the Germans, and study one sentence the way a writer would.
transcripts.wgrd: Today’s reading move is about numbers. A date or a time in a history passage can say more than it seems to. When you see a number, stop and ask what it meant for the people living through it. A few hours. One morning in April. Turn each number into a picture of real people.
transcripts.dol: Today you get to choose which sentence to fix. Both have the same kind of trouble: missing capitals, and two thoughts run together. Pick one, then look back at the model at the top. Notice which words there are names. Names of people, countries, and groups always start tall.
transcripts.guide1: Today’s word work asks you to find things, not just sort them. In grammar and spelling, you’ll hunt through a passage and tap only what fits. That’s harder than it sounds, because the right answers are hiding among ones that look almost right. Slow down, and check each one before you tap.
transcripts.morphology: Yesterday’s first span of the bridge is already built. Today you lay the next four planks. The same two word parts are at work: one means across, and one means forward. Some of these words may be new to you, so let the meaning lead you, not the sound of the word.
transcripts.vocabulary: Today’s words come straight from the reading about Denmark, so you’ll meet them again in just a few minutes. Read the sentence above each one, and look for clues around it. One of these words is about giving up. Another is about the people who run a country. See if you can tell which, before you flip.
transcripts.grammar: In each sentence, more than one of these stand-in words is hiding. Your job is to find only the ones receiving the action, the ones the action happens to. A quick test helps: try swapping in he, or him. If him sounds right, you’ve found one.
transcripts.spelling: Most vowel pairs say what you expect. Today you’re hunting for the ones that don’t. Say each word slowly, and listen. When a pair sits in a part of the word you say quickly, it often goes soft and mumbly. Those are the ones that trip up even grown-up spellers.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Courage Watch is about Denmark’s king, Christian the Tenth. He didn’t fight with weapons. Instead, during the occupation, he kept riding his horse through the streets of Copenhagen, often with no guards around him. People saw him, and knew their king hadn’t given up. Sometimes courage is simply showing up, again and again, where everyone can see you.
transcripts.read: This passage is about how things looked on the surface in Denmark, and what was really going on underneath. Watch for the reason the German leaders had for keeping things calm. Then watch for the people who quietly pushed back. Stop at each pause question before you move on.
transcripts.rwm: Today’s sentence is built in two halves. The first half tells you what someone wanted. Then two small words, so that, turn the corner and give you the reason. Writers use this shape when the why matters as much as the what. When you write your own, make the second half do real work.
transcripts.guide3: Time to write about what you read. Keep the passage close, because each question points back to a part of it. You’ll also study one sentence closely and then try its shape yourself. Then you’ll finish with today’s step in your own writing project.
transcripts.chapter: Two of today’s questions are about differences: how Denmark was treated compared to other countries. A difference needs two sides, so name both. The last question asks about the Resistance. Think about why someone would choose to join, knowing it could be dangerous.
transcripts.workshop: Yesterday you learned that an opinion is something people could disagree with. Today that opinion becomes a claim: one clear sentence that takes a side. No maybe, no kind of. Practice on something you care about, like the best pet or the best season. A clear claim makes everything after it easier.

a.raw: the danes started a resistance they hid jewish people from the nazis
a.fixed: The Danes started a Resistance. They hid Jewish people from the Nazis.
a.why: Capitals on The, Danes, Resistance, Jewish and Nazis, a period after Resistance, a capital T to start the second sentence, and a period at the end.

b.raw: the german army reached copenhagen in april most danes stayed calm
b.why: Capitals on The, German, Copenhagen, April, Most and Danes, a period after April to end the first sentence, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say what you think the Danish people felt that day.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain why the German leaders chose to be gentler at first.
scholar.journal-q3: … and describe one way a quiet act could still be brave.

match.occupation: Occupation is about one country taking control of another. Look for the meaning about taking over.
match.resistance: Resistance means pushing back. Look for the meaning about standing up against something wrong.
match.deport: Deport is about being sent out of a country. Look for the meaning about being forced to leave.
match.rescue: To rescue someone is to get them out of danger. Look for the meaning about saving.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Each right word lays a plank and the bridge reaches forward.

why.t: This week is a bridge between two books, from Anne’s island to Denmark, where Number the Stars takes place. trans- means across, so each word lays a plank across the water. pro- means forward, so the bridge reaches forward, one span each lesson, until it touches the far shore.

wordgame.win: The bridge reaches the far shore, and every lamp is lit. trans- = across, pro- = forward. Next week, the story begins.

notes.wgrd: A date or a number in a history passage can say more than it seems. Stop at each one and turn it into a picture of real people: what did “within a few hours” mean for a family in Denmark?
vocab: To give up and let the other side take control.
To enter a country with an army in order to take it over.
The group of people who run a country and make its rules.
To take someone away by police or soldiers, as a punishment.
When one country takes over and controls another.
Standing up against something you believe is wrong.
To force someone to leave a country, usually against their will.
notes.wordParts: trans- means “across” or “through” (transmit, transport). pro- means “forward” (proclaim, progress).
notes.grammar: Object pronouns receive the action: me, him, her, us, them. To find one, ask who the action happens to. Test: if him sounds right, it’s the object form.
notes.spelling: Most vowel teams say what you expect, but some don’t: eu in neutral says /oo/, and the ai in mountain and certain goes soft because that part of the word is unstressed.
